description: Agro Vista - Bring Nasa data to your field!
summary: Agro Vista helps Vietnamese smallholder farmers decide what to plant next. It reads NASA climate, soil-moisture and vegetation data for the farmer’s exact location, then suggests crop-rotation sequences and explains why each one fits. Farmers often choose crops by habit or rumor, and climate change makes that riskier. Wrong choices lead to depleted soil, crop failure and lost income. Agro Vista turns satellite data into plain-language advice in local units (sào) that works even on a weak connection.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

Agro Vista is a web app that helps farmers choose crops and plan crop-rotation sequences suited to their exact field. It works in four steps:

  1. Pick a location: the user selects a point on the map, uses GPS, or searches by place name.
  2. Collect data: the app pulls climate data from NASA POWER (temperature, rainfall, solar radiation, root-zone soil moisture), the NDVI vegetation index from MODIS, and soil properties from SoilGrids. Forecast and elevation data come from Open-Meteo.
  3. Analyze: the app scores how well 15 common crops fit local conditions, then proposes rotation sequences.
  4. Explain: every sequence comes with a list of reasons it was suggested. Every number shows its source, date and confidence level. An AI assistant explains the results in plain language and can read them aloud.

The app also includes:

  • Reverse verification: the user enters the crop they already plan to grow, and the app checks it against NASA data season by season, not just against the annual average.
  • Water balance: rainfall compared with evaporation, together with root-zone soil moisture.
  • PDF export of the rotation plan to take to the field.
  • Offline mode (PWA): the latest analysis is saved so it can be viewed without internet.
  • Admin dashboard.

2. What benefits does it bring?

  • Farmers get a data-based reason to choose a crop instead of relying on habit or rumor.
  • Proper rotation reduces soil degradation and limits the build-up of pests and disease.
  • It helps avoid crops that don’t suit the season’s water and temperature conditions, lowering the risk of crop failure.
  • Farmers in areas without a nearby extension officer still get evidence-based advice.
  • Results use local units (sào) and familiar Vietnamese soil names, so they are easy to understand and apply.

3. What is the expected impact?

  • For farming households: more stable income, healthier soil over many seasons, and lower costs from choosing the wrong crop or timing.
  • For communities: it opens up NASA’s free satellite data to small-scale agriculture, a group that existing tools rarely serve.
  • For the environment: it encourages sustainable farming and more sensible water use in a changing climate.
  • Next steps: calibrate each crop’s thresholds against provincial extension-service planting calendars, add reference crop prices and yields by region, and expand to other countries.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware or software were used?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, packaged in a single file.
  • Libraries: Leaflet (maps), Chart.js (charts).
  • NASA data: POWER, GIBS, MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI (via ORNL DAAC).
  • Other data: SoilGrids (ISRIC), OpenEPI, Open-Meteo, BigDataCloud, GeoJS.
  • Infrastructure: Firebase (accounts and data), Cloudflare Workers (backend proxy), a service worker (offline mode).
  • IoT: receives sensor data through ThingSpeak when available. 🔧 If your team has real sensor hardware, name the microcontroller and sensors used.
  • AI: a language model running on Groq powers the in-app assistant, and Claude (Anthropic) helped write the code and draft content.

5. How is the project innovative?

  • Seasonal reverse verification: instead of only making suggestions, the app also checks the decision the farmer already has in mind.
  • Transparent data: every number shows its source, date and confidence, so users know what is measured and what is estimated.
  • Reasons behind every recommendation: farmers understand why a crop is suggested instead of receiving a black-box answer.
  • Satellite and ground data combined: NASA POWER, MODIS, SoilGrids and IoT sensors complement each other.
  • True localization: the sào unit, Vietnamese soil names, and a Vietnamese interface and voice.

6. What factors did the team consider?

  • Unreliable data sources: SoilGrids is often slow or unresponsive, so the team built fallbacks to other sources (including IoT sensors) and friendly messages instead of raw errors.
  • Weak connectivity in rural areas: the team added offline mode and saved the latest analysis.
  • Users who are not tech-savvy: a simple interface, friendly dialogs, read-aloud results and familiar units.
  • Reliability: satellite data has limited resolution and some error, so the app shows confidence levels and treats results as recommendations, not a replacement for advice from an extension officer.
  • Role of AI: agronomic decisions are computed from data and crop rules, and AI is used only to explain results.
  • Practicality: the team is continuing to check each crop’s temperature and rainfall thresholds against official extension-service calendars.
